claim: The AcrA-AcrB-TolC complex is a secondary active antiport system in Escherichia coli, powered by the electrochemical proton gradient across the inner membrane.
source: The AcrA-AcrB-TolC complex is a secondary active antiport system in Escherichia coli, powered by the electrochemical proton gradient across the inner membrane of this Gram-negative bacterium (Okusu et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Okusu et al., 1996, which provides external evidence for this statement.

claim: The AcrAB-TolC system confers multidrug resistance to important pathogenic bacteria involved in human disease.
source: The AcrAB-TolC system and its homologues are also of considerable biomedical interest, as they confer multidrug resistance to important pathogenic bacteria involved in human disease (Nikaido and Pagès, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nikaido and Pagès, 2012.

claim: AcrB belongs to the resistance-nodulation-cell-division (RND) family.
source: This membrane protein belongs to the resistance-nodulation-cell-division (RND) family (Tseng et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tseng et al., 1999.

claim: NPC1 and Patched play key roles in the regulation of cholesterol metabolism and in the Hedgehog signaling pathway of embryonic cells, respectively.
source: In humans, the RND transporters NPC1 and Patched play key roles in the regulation of cholesterol metabolism and in the Hedgehog signaling pathway of embryonic cells, respectively (Taipale et al., 2002; Scott and Ioannou, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Taipale et al., 2002 and Scott and Ioannou, 2004.

claim: The first known structure of AcrB revealed a homotrimeric assembly in which all protomers adopt the same conformation at 3.5 Å resolution.
source: The first known structure of AcrB, solved by X-ray crystallography at a resolution of 3.5 Å, revealed a homotrimeric assembly in which all protomers adopt the same conformation (Murakami et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Murakami et al., 2002.

claim: The transmembrane domain of AcrB consists of 12 α-helices (TM1–TM12).
source: In each protomer, the transmembrane (TM) domain consists of 12 α-helices (TM1–TM12), mostly interconnected by short unstructured loops as is common.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the structure of AcrB.

claim: AcrB features two large periplasmic insertions, between TM1 and TM2, and between TM7 and TM8, which account for approximately 60% of the 1049 amino acids in each protomer.
source: In contrast to other secondary transporters, however, AcrB also features two large periplasmic insertions, between TM1 and TM2, and between TM7 and TM8, which account for approximately 60% of the 1049 amino acids in each protomer.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the structure of AcrB.

claim: The periplasmic insertions project 70 Å away from the membrane.
source: These insertions are highly structured domains that project 70 Å away from the membrane, and form extensive interfaces among protomers (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and references Figure 1.

claim: TolC is 140 Å in length.
source: The more distal region of the periplasmic domain features a central funnel-shaped cavity that channels the substrate towards TolC, the outer-membrane channel component (140 Å in length) of this transport system (Koronakis et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text with a citation to Koronakis et al., 2000.

claim: Upon substrate loading, AcrB becomes asymmetric, with each protomer in the trimer adopting one of three distinct conformational states designated as 'loose' (L), 'tight' (T) and 'open' (O).
source: These structures, however, also revealed that upon substrate loading AcrB becomes asymmetric, that is, each protomer in the trimer adopts one of three distinct conformational states, designated as 'loose' (L), 'tight' (T) and 'open' (O), or alternatively, as 'access', 'binding' and 'extrusion', (Murakami et al., 2006; Seeger et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Murakami et al., 2006 and Seeger et al., 2006.

claim: Drug recognition and efflux are mediated by a sub-domain of the periplasmic region, referred to as the porter domain, whose mechanism is akin to that of a peristaltic pump.
source: On the basis of these structures as well as other findings (Seeger et al., 2008; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2009), it has also become generally accepted that drug recognition and efflux are mediated by a sub-domain of the periplasmic region, referred to as the porter domain (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), whose mechanism is akin to that of a peristaltic pump (Seeger et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Seeger et al., 2008, Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2009, and Seeger et al., 2006.

claim: Recognition of high molecular-mass drugs occurs in the L state, via an access pocket in the porter domain that is open to the periplasmic space.
source: Specifically, recognition of high molecular-mass drugs occurs in the L state, via an access pocket in the porter domain that is open to the periplasmic space (Nakashima et al., 2011; Eicher et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nakashima et al., 2011 and Eicher et al., 2012.

claim: Low molecular-mass drugs can bind directly to the deep binding pocket in the T protomer without binding to the access pocket first.
source: When the L protomer transitions to the T state, drugs translocate to a binding pocket deeper in the protein; low molecular-mass drugs, however, can apparently bind directly to the deep binding pocket in the T protomer without binding to the access pocket first (Nakashima et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nakashima et al., 2011.

claim: Drug extrusion occurs in the transition from T to O.
source: Drug extrusion occurs next, in the transition from T to O, which re-shapes and opens the binding pocket to a central cavity in the funnel domain, which leads to the lumen of the TolC channel.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the mechanism.

claim: The O to L transition resets the conformational cycle by re-exposing the binding site to the periplasm.
source: Finally, the O to L transition resets the conformational cycle by re-exposing the binding site to the periplasm.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the mechanism.

claim: Recent measurements of AcrB transport kinetics are consistent with a bi-site activation model.
source: Indeed, recent measurements of AcrB transport kinetics (Nagano and Nikaido, 2009; Lim and Nikaido, 2010) are consistent with a bi-site activation model (Pos, 2009), analogous to the binding-change mechanism of the ATP synthase (Boyer, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nagano and Nikaido, 2009, Lim and Nikaido, 2010, Pos, 2009, and Boyer, 1997.

claim: The TM domain consists of two 5-helix parallel repeats, referred to as R1 and R2, and two flanking helices, TM2 and TM8.
source: Our analysis indicates that the TM domain consists of two 5-helix parallel repeats, referred to as R1 and R2, and two flanking helices, TM2 and TM8.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A. The analysis is based on structural data from the manuscript.

claim: R1 includes TM1 and TM3 to TM6, while R2 comprises TM7 and TM9 to TM12.
source: The N-terminal repeat, R1, includes TM1 and TM3 to TM6, while the C-terminal repeat, R2, comprises TM7 and TM9 to TM12 (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and references Figure 1.

claim: The porter domain consists of two structural repeats, referred to as PN1/PC2, and PN2/PC1.
source: In the porter domain, as noted previously, each protomer consists of two structural repeats, referred to as PN1/PC2, and PN2/PC1 (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and references figures.

claim: The PN1/PC2 repeat appears to be a rigid unit throughout the LTO conformational cycle with RMSD among states of less than 0.5 Å.
source: The PN1/PC2 repeat appears to be a rigid unit throughout the LTO conformational cycle. Analysis of the conformation of this repeat in the 1.9 Å-resolution crystal structure of wildtype AcrB (Eicher et al., 2012) yields root-mean-square differences (RMSD) among states of less than 0.5 Å (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on RMSD analysis of the crystal structure data.

claim: The PN2/PC1 tandem changes its conformation significantly, with RMSD of approximately 2.0 Å in the L to T transition and approximately 1.8 Å in the T to O transition.
source: By contrast, the PN2/PC1 tandem changes its conformation significantly, in particular in the L to T (RMSD ∼2.0 Å) and T to O transitions (RMSD ∼1.8 Å).
evidence: The claim is based on RMSD analysis of the crystal structure data.

claim: The conformation of the funnel domain is largely unchanged throughout the cycle with RMSD < 0.5 Å.
source: Incidentally, the conformation of the funnel domain is largely unchanged throughout the cycle (RMSD < 0.5 Å).
evidence: The claim is based on RMSD analysis of the crystal structure data.

claim: The structure of the R1 five-helix bundle is largely preserved in the L, T and O conformations with RMSD ranging from 0.8 to 1.1 Å.
source: Analysis of R1, for example, shows that the structure of this five-helix bundle is largely preserved in the L, T and O conformations; the RMSD among these states ranges from 0.8 to 1.1 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on RMSD analysis of the crystal structure data.

claim: The structure of R2 is even more preserved than R1, with RMSD values between 0.3 and 1.0 Å.
source: These differences are even smaller for R2, with RMSD values between 0.3 and 1.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on RMSD analysis of the crystal structure data.

claim: R1 and R2 are always different from each other with RMSD approximately 3.5 Å.
source: R1 and R2 are, however, always different from each other (RMSD ∼3.5 Å).
evidence: The claim is based on RMSD analysis of the crystal structure data.

claim: R1 and R2 move relative to each other throughout the conformational cycle of each protomer.
source: Further inspection also shows that R1 and R2 move relative to each other throughout the conformational cycle of each protomer (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure data.

claim: In the L to T transition, R1 and R2 undergo a rocking motion around an axis that is tilted relative to the membrane plane.
source: In the L to T transition, R1 and R2 undergo a rocking motion around an axis that is tilted relative to the membrane plane (Figure 3; Video 4).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3 and Video 4.

claim: In the transition between the T and O states, and between O and L, R1 and R2 undergo mostly a lateral shear motion relative to each other.
source: By contrast, in the transition between the T and O states, and between O and L, what can be observed is mostly a lateral shear motion of R1 and R2, relative to each other (Figure 3; Video 5, Video 6).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3, Video 5, and Video 6.

claim: In the L to T transition, TM2 moves downwards relative to R1 (toward the cytoplasm), returning to the up state in the O conformation.
source: In the L to T transition, TM2 moves downwards relative to R1 (toward the cytoplasm), returning to the up state in the O conformation (Figure 3; Video 4, Video 5, Video 6).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3 and videos.

claim: TM8 is similarly positioned in the L and T states, and largely unengaged from R2.
source: By contrast, TM8 is similarly positioned in the L and T states, and largely unengaged from R2.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure data.

claim: During the T to O transition, TM8 becomes closely packed against R2, through hydrophobic interactions with TM5.
source: However, during the T to O transition this α-helix becomes closely packed against R2, through hydrophobic interactions with TM5.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure data.

claim: In the T to O transition, TM8 becomes elongated, reaching directly to the PN1/PC2 unit.
source: In this transition TM8 also becomes elongated, reaching directly to the PN1/PC2 unit (Figure 3; Video 4, Video 5, Video 6).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3 and videos.

claim: Iα functions as a connecting rod coupling the displacements of TM2 and R2.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that Iα functions as a connecting rod coupling the displacements of TM2 and R2.
evidence: The claim is based on RMSD analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: D407, D408, K940, and R971 are critical for function.
source: In particular D407 and D408 in TM4 and K940 in TM10 are critical for function (Guan and Nakae, 2001; Murakami and Yamaguchi, 2003; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2006; Seeger et al., 2009). Another functionally important side-chain, R971 in TM11, is located about 10 Å away from K940 on TM10, towards the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guan and Nakae, 2001, Murakami and Yamaguchi, 2003, Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2006, and Seeger et al., 2009.

claim: In both the L and T states, R1 and R2 are strongly paired through multiple interactions including K940 sandwiched between D407 and D408.
source: In both the L and T states, R1 and R2 appear to be strongly paired through multiple interactions. First, through K940, which projects away from R2 and is sandwiched between D407 and D408, from R1, forming two simultaneous ionic interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the high-resolution crystal structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the O state, all R1-R2 interactions break off, and are replaced by alternative ones within each repeat.
source: In the O state, by contrast, all R1-R2 interactions break off, and are replaced by alternative ones within each repeat.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the high-resolution crystal structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: D407 and D408 are ionized in the L and T states but become protonated in the O state.
source: These include D407 and D408, in the core of the TM domain, which are ionized in the L and T states but become protonated in the O state (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on Monte Carlo simulations of protonation equilibrium shown in Figure 5.

claim: E346 and D924 are protonated in the L and T states, but become deprotonated in O.
source: Interestingly, E346 and D924, at the periplasmic end of TM2 and TM10, respectively, are protonated in the L and T states, but become deprotonated in O
evidence: The claim is based on Monte Carlo simulations of protonation equilibrium shown in Figure 5.

claim: H338 and D566 are most likely deprotonated in L and T, and become protonated in the O state.
source: conversely, the neighboring H338 (TM2) and D566 (in the region between TM7 and PC1 subdomain) are most likely deprotonated in L and T, and become protonated in the O state (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on Monte Carlo simulations of protonation equilibrium shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both K940 and R971 remain protonated throughout the cycle.
source: Lastly, the calculations indicate that both K940 and R971 remain protonated throughout the cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on Monte Carlo simulations of protonation equilibrium.

claim: All-atom molecular simulations and continuum-electrostatic calculations indicate that in the L and T states, two protons are bound to the TM domain of AcrB at the periplasmic side (D924 and E346), while D407 and D408 are deprotonated.
source: In sum, both all-atom molecular simulations and continuum-electrostatic calculations indicate that in the L and T states, two protons are bound to the TM domain of AcrB at the periplasmic side (i.e., D924 and E346), while D407 and D408, two-thirds of the way across the membrane, are deprotonated
evidence: The claim is based on computational analysis including Monte Carlo simulations and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Upon transition to the O state, two protons bind to D407 and D408, while the proton-accepting sites on the periplasmic face become deprotonated.
source: upon transition to the O state, two protons bind to D407 and D408, while the proton-accepting sites on the periplasmic face become deprotonated.
evidence: The claim is based on computational analysis including Monte Carlo simulations and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The primary role of K940 and R971 is to function as a conformational electrostatic switch coupled to the protonation state of D407 and D408.
source: Our results suggest that the primary role of these side-chains is not, however, to capture and donate protons; instead, they appear to function as a conformational electrostatic switch coupled to the protonation state of D407 and D408.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from computational analysis and structural data.

claim: The re-configuration of the reversible electrostatic switch, coupled to the protonation and deprotonation of both D407 and D408, is the trigger for the lateral displacements of repeat R2 relative to R1 observed in the T to O and O to L transitions.
source: We propose that the re-configuration of this reversible electrostatic switch, which is coupled to the protonation and deprotonation of both D407 and D408, is the trigger for the lateral displacements of repeat R2 relative to R1 observed in the T to O and O to L transitions (Figure 3; Video 5, Video 6).
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on inference from computational and structural data.

claim: Crystal structures of K940A, R971A, D407N and D408N variants were solved at resolutions ranging from 2.0 to 2.3 Å.
source: To further assess the proposed proton-relay mechanism and its influence on the conformation of the TM domain, we solved the atomic structures of four AcrB variants, namely K940A, R971A, D407N and D408N (Supplementary file 2), all of which abolish the drug-efflux activity of AcrB (Guan and Nakae, 2001; Murakami and Yamaguchi, 2003; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2006; Seeger et al., 2009). Electron-density maps for these variants could be resolved at resolutions ranging from 2.0 to 2.3 Å
evidence: The claim is based on X-ray crystallography data reported in the manuscript.

claim: All four variants (K940A, R971A, D407N, D408N) abolish the drug-efflux activity of AcrB.
source: we solved the atomic structures of four AcrB variants, namely K940A, R971A, D407N and D408N (Supplementary file 2), all of which abolish the drug-efflux activity of AcrB (Guan and Nakae, 2001; Murakami and Yamaguchi, 2003; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2006; Seeger et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guan and Nakae, 2001, Murakami and Yamaguchi, 2003, Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2006, and Seeger et al., 2009.

claim: In all variant crystal structures, the crystal structures represent an asymmetric configuration of the AcrB trimer.
source: In all cases, the crystal structures represent an asymmetric configuration of the AcrB trimer.
evidence: The claim is based on X-ray crystallography data of the variants.

claim: None of the substitutions studied caused significant changes in the internal structure of the R1 and R2 repeats, compared to the wildtype L, T and O states.
source: None of the substitutions studied caused significant changes in the internal structure of the R1 and R2 repeats, compared to the wildtype L, T and O states (Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison of variant and wildtype structures.

claim: The relative orientation of R1 and R2 is unchanged in the K940A and D408N mutants.
source: The relative orientation of these two repeats is also unchanged in the K940A and D408N mutants (Supplementary file 3C)
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison of variant and wildtype structures.

claim: In the K940A structure, D408 is constitutively neutralized throughout the cycle.
source: Indeed, electrostatic calculations analogous to those carried out for the wildtype protein show that in the K940A structure, D408 is constitutively neutralized throughout the cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on electrostatic calculations shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In K940A, D407 is deprotonated in the L and T states and protonated in the O state, as in the wildtype.
source: D407, which is more proximal to R971, is deprotonated in the L and T states and protonated in the O state, as in the wildtype (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on electrostatic calculations shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The T state in the crystal structures of the R971A and D407N mutants is an intermediate between the T and O conformations in wildtype AcrB.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis that the structural configuration of the proton-relay network is intimately coupled to the displacements of the 5-helix repeats, the arrangement of these repeats in the T protomer of the R971A crystal structure is an intermediate between the T and O states of the wildtype structure (Figure 8); in fact, this altered conformation is more similar to the latter (RMSD values of 2.4 vs 1.6 Å, respectively—Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 8 and Supplementary file 3C.

claim: The L state permits the formation of two persistent water channels open to the cytoplasm, at the interface between repeats R1 and R2, reaching into the proton-binding site; access from the periplasmic space is closed.
source: More specifically, we observe that the L state permits the formation of two persistent water channels open to the cytoplasm, at the interface between repeats R1 and R2, and reaching into the proton-binding site; access from the periplasmic space is, however, closed (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is based on all-atom molecular dynamics simulation analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In the T state, two narrow water wires form on the periplasmic face of the TM domain, reaching into the proton-binding site.
source: In the T state, by contrast, two narrow water wires form on the periplasmic face of the TM domain, again reaching into the proton-binding site, and approximately along the interface between the two repeats R1 and R2 (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is based on all-atom molecular dynamics simulation analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: E346 and D924 flank the entrance of each of the periplasmic water wires in the T state.
source: Interestingly, E346 and D924 flank the entrance of each of these water wires
evidence: The claim is based on all-atom molecular dynamics simulation analysis.

claim: E346 and D924 facilitate proton uptake by providing transient binding sites en route to D407/D408.
source: as mentioned earlier, both these side-chains are likely to be protonated in the L and T states and deprotonated in the O state (Figure 4, Figure 5), which suggests that E346 and D924 facilitate proton uptake by providing transient binding sites en route to D407/D408 (Fischer and Kandt, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from computational analysis and is supported by a citation to Fischer and Kandt, 2011.

claim: The O state features two water channels into the proton-binding site that are highly similar to those seen in the L conformation, open to the cytoplasm, while access from the periplasmic space is occluded.
source: Finally, the O state features two water channels into the proton-binding site that are highly similar to those seen in the L conformation, that is, open to the cytoplasm, while access from the periplasmic space is also occluded (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is based on all-atom molecular dynamics simulation analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Throughout the conformational cycle of AcrB the proton-binding sites within the TM domain become alternately accessible to the periplasm or the cytoplasm.
source: In sum, our data indicate that throughout the conformational cycle of AcrB the proton-binding sites within the TM domain become alternately accessible to the periplasm or the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Two distinct types of relative motion of repeats R1 and R2 result in alternating access, namely a rocking motion during the L to T transition, with no protons bound, and a shear motion in the T to O transition, in the protonated form.
source: Interestingly, two distinct types of relative motion of repeats R1 and R2 result in alternating access, namely a rocking motion during the L to T transition, with no protons bound, and a shear motion in the T to O transition, in the protonated form.
evidence: The claim is based on structural and computational analysis.

claim: AcrB is the only secondary-transporter for which two distinct structural transitions resulting in alternating access have been described to date.
source: To our knowledge, however, AcrB is the only secondary-transporter for which two distinct structural transitions resulting in alternating access have been described to date.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Proton uptake leads to substrate export (instead of symport) because both proton- and substrate-binding sites are concurrently open to the periplasm in the T state, while in the O state they become open to the cytoplasm and the TolC lumen, respectively.
source: Proton uptake leads to substrate export (instead of symport) for two reasons: first, both proton- and substrate-binding sites are concurrently open to the periplasm in the T state, while in the O state they become open to the cytoplasm and the TolC lumen, respectively
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural and computational analysis.

claim: Both porter and membrane domains are able to re-open to the periplasm after releasing their cargo, in their apo state.
source: second, both porter and membrane domains are able to re-open to the periplasm after releasing their cargo, that is, in their apo state (Figure 11A, drug access pocket and proton loading).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural and computational analysis shown in Figure 11A.

claim: The free-energy gain associated with downhill proton permeation compensates the cost of uphill efflux of cytotoxic compounds.
source: Thus, the free-energy gain associated with downhill proton permeation compensates the cost of uphill efflux of cytotoxic compounds.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the proposed mechanism.

claim: Transport of certain cephalosporins and penicillins has been shown to be highly cooperative.
source: Indeed, transport of certain cephalosporins and penicillins has been shown to be highly cooperative (Nagano and Nikaido, 2009; Lim and Nikaido, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nagano and Nikaido, 2009 and Lim and Nikaido, 2010.

claim: Analysis of computer-generated models of the porter domain in all non-symmetric permutations of the L, T and O states indicates that OO and LO interfaces are highly incompatible, and that OT is also suboptimal.
source: Remarkably, analysis of computer-generated models of the porter domain in all non-symmetric permutations of the L, T and O states ('Materials and methods') indicates that this kind of kinetic optimization is what emerges from the conformational coupling among protomers. A quantification of the steric clashes between protomers in these hypothetical models indicates that OO and LO interfaces (counter-clockwise, viewed from TolC) are highly incompatible, and that OT is also suboptimal.
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: Throughout the proposed conformational cycle, the proportion of protomers in either the L or T state relative to those in the O state is fourfold greater than in a hypothetical uncoupled trimer.
source: Throughout this cycle, the proportion of protomers in either the L or T state relative to those in the O state is fourfold greater than in a hypothetical uncoupled trimer (Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: The AcrB protomers are substantially more efficient efflux pumps if they are coupled, not because the protomers energize each other, but because collectively they are able to restrict their conformational pathways so as to achieve the most productive mechanism.
source: That is, the AcrB protomers are substantially more efficient efflux pumps if they are coupled; not because the protomers energize each other, but because collectively they are able to restrict their conformational pathways so as to achieve the most productive mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the computational modeling analysis.

claim: The mechanism of AcrB involves two remote alternating-access conformational cycles within each protomer, namely one for protons in the transmembrane region and another for drugs in the periplasmic domain, 50 Å apart.
source: Analysis of wildtype AcrB and four functionally-inactive variants reveals an unprecedented mechanism that involves two remote alternating-access conformational cycles within each protomer, namely one for protons in the transmembrane region and another for drugs in the periplasmic domain, 50 Å apart.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is based on the comprehensive analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Each of the alternating-access cycles entails two distinct types of collective motions of two structural repeats, coupled by flanking α-helices that project from the membrane.
source: Each of these cycles entails two distinct types of collective motions of two structural repeats, coupled by flanking α-helices that project from the membrane.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is based on the structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cross-talk among protomers across the trimerization interface might lead to a more kinetically efficient efflux system.
source: Moreover, we rationalize how the cross-talk among protomers across the trimerization interface might lead to a more kinetically efficient efflux system.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is based on the computational modeling analysis presented in the manuscript.
